entries.definition: A thin translation layer between two interfaces or systems.
entries.plain: A converter between two contracts.
entries.example: Translate a provider-specific agent protocol into an internal interface.

entries.definition: Software placed around another API, library or system to expose a simpler or different interface.
entries.plain: A layer around something else.
entries.example: A Python library may mostly wrap a REST API.

entries.definition: Using your own product internally in real work.
entries.plain: Use what you build yourself.
entries.example: A coding-agent team uses its own agent to develop the agent.

entries.definition: Building software primarily by describing desired changes to AI coding tools rather than manually writing most code.
entries.plain: Drive coding through natural-language intent.
entries.example: Describe a feature, let the agent implement it, then inspect the result.

entries.definition: Derogatory term for low-quality, repetitive or mass-generated AI content.
entries.plain: Cheap AI output with little judgment or verification.
entries.example: Generated documentation that sounds plausible but says nothing useful.

entries.definition: Small amounts of code written mainly to connect existing components.
entries.plain: Code that makes other pieces fit together.
entries.example: Translate one tool result into the input format another component expects.

entries.definition: Informal term for infrastructure that moves data or control between components.
entries.plain: The unglamorous connectivity that makes the system work.
entries.example: Tool routing, serialization, state transport and callbacks.

entries.definition: Solving a chain of prerequisite problems that pulls you away from the original task.
entries.plain: You started fixing one thing and ended up fixing five unrelated setup problems.
entries.example: Fix test → update dependency → repair Docker → rebuild CI.

entries.definition: An investigation that keeps expanding into deeper or increasingly unrelated issues.
entries.plain: You keep going deeper and lose the original scope.
entries.example: A minor bug leads to redesigning the whole architecture.

entries.definition: Spending disproportionate time debating trivial details while more important problems remain.
entries.plain: Arguing about easy details instead of hard decisions.
entries.example: Debating naming for an hour while the API contract is still undefined.

entries.definition: A feature that makes it easy to accidentally cause serious problems.
entries.plain: A dangerous capability that is too easy to misuse.
entries.example: An unrestricted recursive delete tool exposed to an agent.

entries.definition: A feature or behavior that works but is easy to misuse or misunderstand.
entries.plain: Something likely to hurt you if handled carelessly.
entries.example: An API silently accepts ambiguous units.

entries.definition: The normal scenario where inputs and dependencies behave as expected.
entries.plain: Everything goes right.
entries.example: Valid input, network available and tools succeed.

entries.definition: An uncommon condition that can expose failures not visible in normal operation.
entries.plain: A weird but possible case.
entries.example: An empty selection or extremely large input file.

entries.definition: Standard repetitive code or configuration required to set something up.
entries.plain: Necessary setup that contains little unique logic.
entries.example: Project configuration generated for every new service.

entries.definition: Behavior that happens implicitly and is difficult to see or explain.
entries.plain: The framework does something behind the scenes.
entries.example: Automatic tool discovery with no obvious configuration.

entries.definition: A system understood mainly through its inputs and outputs without inspecting internal implementation.
entries.plain: Judge what it does from the outside.
entries.example: Characterize a closed sensor algorithm by controlled inputs and measured outputs.

entries.definition: A system analyzed with access to its internal implementation and structure.
entries.plain: You can inspect how it works inside.
entries.example: Debug an algorithm by reading its source and internal state.

entries.definition: Informal term for excessive or unnecessary tool calls by an agent.
entries.plain: The agent keeps calling tools without enough purpose.
entries.example: Repeatedly reading the same files without new evidence.

entries.definition: Informal term for consuming large numbers of model tokens unnecessarily.
entries.plain: Wasting model budget.
entries.example: Re-reading the entire repository on every iteration.

entries.definition: An instruction system that keeps adding prompt rules to patch behavior until it becomes hard to understand or maintain.
entries.plain: Too many rules stuffed into prompts.
entries.example: A 20-page prompt compensates for missing policies, tests and hooks.

entries.definition: A multi-agent architecture with too many agents, handoffs and unclear responsibilities.
entries.plain: More agents created more complexity than capability.
entries.example: Five agents debate a task that one well-tooled agent could execute.

entries.definition: Adding architecture, abstractions or infrastructure beyond what the problem requires.
entries.plain: Building more system than you need.
entries.example: Adding a database, queue and microservices for a static personal glossary.
